subject: Surgery
summary: A hernia is the protrusion of an organ or tissue through a defect in its containing wall. Diagnosis relies on history and focused exam, with imaging when the presentation is unclear.

sections.p: A hernia occurs when a structure (usually bowel) pushes through a weakness or opening in the abdominal wall or related fascia. Diagnosis is clinical: a palpable, often reducible bulge that enlarges with strain and may be tender if incarcerated.
b: Irreducible bulge, pain, or signs of obstruction suggest incarceration.
Visible or palpable defect with cough impulse supports diagnosis.

sections.p: Hernias are staged by reducibility and complications: reducible, incarcerated (cannot be reduced), and strangulated (vascular compromise). Strangulation is a surgical emergency.
b: Reducible – can be pushed back, no acute symptoms.
Incarcerated – trapped, may cause obstruction.
Strangulated – ischemia, risk of necrosis, requires urgent surgery.

sections.p: Most hernias arise from a combination of congenital weakness and acquired stressors. In low‑resource settings, chronic cough (TB), heavy lifting, and malnutrition increase risk.
b: Congenital fascial defects (e.g., indirect inguinal).
Increased intra‑abdominal pressure (chronic cough, constipation, pregnancy).
Previous surgery or trauma causing fascial disruption.
Infections that weaken tissue (TB, schistosomiasis).

sections.p: Patients notice a bulge that may enlarge with coughing, standing, or straining. Pain is usually mild unless incarceration or strangulation occurs, which adds tenderness, nausea, vomiting, and obstipation.
b: Bulge that reduces when supine.
Painful, firm, non‑reducible mass → possible incarceration.
Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia) → possible strangulation.

sections.p: Imaging confirms the diagnosis when the exam is equivocal or to assess complications.

t.b: Is the mass a hernia and is it reducible? → Shows fascial defect and contents; dynamic exam can demonstrate reducibility.
Is there bowel obstruction or strangulation? → Shows dilated loops, wall thickening, reduced enhancement; guides urgency of surgery.
Is there obstruction? → Dilated loops with air‑fluid levels; may be normal if hernia is not obstructed.

sections.p: Complications arise from loss of blood supply or bowel obstruction, leading to sepsis and death if untreated.
b: Severe, constant pain with a hard, tender mass.
Vomiting, obstipation, or abdominal distension.
Fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis indicating strangulation.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and repair the defect. Non‑operative reduction may be attempted for some reducible hernias, but definitive repair is surgical.
b: Analgesia and anti‑emetics for symptom control.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics if strangulation suspected (cover gram‑negative and anaerobes).
Elective herniorrhaphy: mesh repair for most adult inguinal/ventral hernias; tissue repair for contaminated fields.

sections.p: Post‑operative wound care and activity modification reduce recurrence. Address risk factors such as chronic cough, constipation, and heavy lifting.
b: Encourage gradual return to activity; avoid lifting >10 kg for 4–6 weeks.
Treat chronic cough (TB, COPD) and constipation.
Weight control and smoking cessation.

sections.p: Other abdominal wall swellings can mimic hernias.
b: Lipoma – soft, mobile, no cough impulse.
Femoral hernia – below inguinal ligament, higher strangulation risk.
Abdominal wall abscess – tender, erythematous, may have fluctuance.

sections.p: Imaging may miss a small defect or underestimate strangulation.
b: Ultrasound may be operator‑dependent; a negative study does not exclude a hernia.
CT can show a reducible hernia that later becomes incarcerated; clinical assessment remains paramount.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe, constant abdominal pain with a hard, non‑reducible bulge
Vomiting, inability to pass stool or gas, abdominal distension
Fever, rapid heart rate, or signs of sepsis

faq.q: Can a hernia be treated without surgery?
faq.a: Small, reducible hernias may be observed, but definitive repair is recommended to prevent incarceration; non‑surgical reduction is only temporary.

faq.q: Why is mesh preferred for most adult repairs?
faq.a: Mesh provides tension‑free reinforcement, lowering recurrence compared with tissue‑only repair.

faq.q: What makes a femoral hernia more dangerous than an inguinal hernia?
faq.a: Its narrow canal predisposes to rapid strangulation, so urgent repair is advised.

exam: Describe the clinical features that differentiate a reducible from a strangulated inguinal hernia.
Explain the role of imaging in evaluating a suspected incarcerated hernia and its limitations.
Outline the management steps for a patient presenting with a strangulated ventral hernia.
